people.scope: Black Americans, including people of the Black diaspora from the Caribbean, Latin America, Canada and Europe, and Americans whose parents came from those places. People born on the African continent are outside this page’s scope.
people.counting: Each person is counted once per line, in the year of their first recorded founding or patent/invention.

scf.label: Federal Reserve Survey of Consumer Finances (SCF)
scf.note: 1989–2019 converted from the Fed’s 2022-dollar table to 2025 dollars with the factor the Fed’s own 2022 figures imply (×1.0943). 2022 and 2025 are the Fed-published 2025-dollar values.

sources.name: Federal Reserve, FEDS Notes (Oct 2023): Greater Wealth, Greater Uncertainty
The Emancipator (Oct 19, 2026), reporting the Fed’s 2025 SCF

longrun.label: White-to-Black per-capita wealth ratio (Derenoncourt, Kim, Kuhn & Schularick)
longrun.note: Per-capita wealth across all Black and white Americans. This is a different measure from the SCF median-household ratio, so the two lines are drawn separately and should not be joined.

sources.name: NBER Working Paper 30101, Wealth of Two Nations: The U.S. Racial Wealth Gap, 1860–2020

crosscheck.source: Pew Research Center analysis of Census SIPP data (2011)
crosscheck.finding: White-to-Black and White-to-Hispanic median wealth ratios were about 10 to 1 from 1984 to 2004, then about 20 to 1 (Black) and 18 to 1 (Hispanic) in 2009.
crosscheck.differs: The Fed SCF puts the 2010 White-to-Black ratio near 8 to 1. SIPP records less wealth at the top and changed its design in 1996 and its race question in 2004, so it runs higher than SCF.

crosscheck.source: Derenoncourt et al. vs. Fed SCF (2019)
crosscheck.finding: Per-capita ratio 6.6 to 1 (DKKS) vs. median-household ratio 7.8 to 1 (SCF) for the same year.
crosscheck.differs: Means and per-person figures are pulled up by large Black fortunes and family size; medians track the typical household.

crosscheck.finding: Black median wealth fell 25% (2022→2025) while White rose 6% and Hispanic 18%, pushing the White-to-Black ratio to about 9 to 1, the widest since 2016.
crosscheck.differs: CEPR economist Algernon Austin suggests falling home, vehicle and retirement values and expired COVID-era relief; the Fed has not confirmed causes.

source.name: Federal Reserve Distributional Financial Accounts (wealth by race)

externalProjections.who: Institute for Policy Studies & Prosperity Now (2017), The Road to Zero Wealth
externalProjections.claim: If 1983–2013 trends continued, Black median wealth would reach zero by 2053 and Latino by 2073.
externalProjections.check: Later Fed data ran the other way through 2022 (Black median up to $49,100 in 2025 dollars) before falling 25% by 2025. Treat as a scenario, not a forecast.

externalProjections.claim: With today’s wealth-building conditions, the White-to-Black per-capita gap stops closing; convergence would take centuries without equal capital gains and savings conditions.
externalProjections.check: Their measured gap has stayed between 5 and 7 to 1 for 70 years.

externalProjections.claim: The Hispanic share of U.S. wealth could roughly triple by 2025, driven by population growth.
externalProjections.check: Hispanic median wealth did rise faster than any group 2019–2025 (SCF), but stayed under one-quarter of White median wealth.
